crywolf

Bayesian false-positive occupancy models for data from automated detectors, with simulation-based checks of whether the correction is calibrated for your design.

Acoustic classifiers and other automated detectors return false positives. crywolf fits the multiple-methods (site-confirmation) false-positive occupancy model of Miller et al. (2011) in Stan: the classifier output may be wrong, and a verified subset of detections is certain. It also fits the observation-confirmation design of Chambert et al. (2015), in which an expert checks the observations of some automated occasions. The false-positive rate can be constant or depend on site covariates, which matters when false positives track the same environmental gradient as the species.

Installation

crywolf is distributed through R-universe, which provides binaries for Windows, macOS and Linux. The command below also installs ‘cmdstanr’ from the Stan R-universe; CmdStan itself is installed once with install_cmdstan():

install.packages("crywolf", repos = c("https://diogoprov.r-universe.dev",
                                      "https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev",
                                      getOption("repos")))
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()

The development version can be installed from GitHub with remotes::install_github("diogoprov/crywolf").

Example 

library(crywolf)

# simulated data in which false positives track a gradient correlated
# with the occupancy covariate
sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 300, nocc = 20, conf_effect = 1.5,
                   conf_cor = 0.7, seed = 2026)

# the simulated recorders have no effect, so leave the recorder term out
m0 <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE)  # constant rate
m1 <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ x, random_recorder = FALSE)  # rate depends on x

coef(m0, "occ"); coef(m1, "occ")                # true slope: -0.8
loo::loo_compare(loo(m0), loo(m1))

# is a constant rate calibrated for this design, and does verifying more help?
fp_verification_curve(nsite = 300, nocc = 20, conf_effect = 1.5,
                      conf_cor = 0.7,
                      models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_on_x = ~ x),
                      reps = 50)

Main functions

Function Purpose
fp_data(), fp_data_wide() assemble automated, verified, and confirmed detections and site covariates
fp_occu() fit the model; methods print, summary, coef, predict, loo, as_draws_df
fp_ppc() posterior predictive check of the detections per site
fp_priors() prior settings
simulate_fp() simulate data under homogeneous, unstructured, or structured false positives
fp_calibrate() coverage and bias of the credible intervals for a design, by simulation
fp_verification_curve() coverage against the fraction of sites verified
plot() coverage or bias of a calibration run
curiango acoustic monitoring of the Common Pauraque in the Pantanal (Piatti et al. 2026)

Related tools

  • fpcalib is the research compendium of the simulation study behind the calibration checks (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23379100). simulate_fp(seed = s) reproduces its datasets exactly.
  • birdnet-validation-sampler (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22696210) cuts audio clips from BirdNET predictions for manual review and records the verdict on each clip, which can feed the verified or confirmed data of fp_data(). The models in crywolf treat the checked recordings as chosen independently of the classifier’s confidence score. Clips picked because they have the highest scores contain fewer false positives than a random sample and would understate the false-positive rate, so draw the clips at random for this use.

Citation

If you use crywolf, please cite the package (citation("crywolf"); https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23385045, which always resolves to the latest version) and Miller et al. (2011), or Chambert et al. (2015) for the observation-confirmation design.

Miller, D. A., Nichols, J. D., McClintock, B. T., Grant, E. H. C., Bailey, L. L., & Weir, L. A. (2011). Improving occupancy estimation when two types of observational error occur: non-detection and species misidentification. Ecology, 92, 1422–1428. https://doi.org/10.1890/10-1396.1

Chambert, T., Miller, D. A. W., & Nichols, J. D. (2015). Modeling false positive detections in species occurrence data under different study designs. Ecology, 96, 332–339. https://doi.org/10.1890/14-1507.1

Why “crywolf”?

The name comes from Aesop’s fable The Boy Who Cried Wolf (Perry Index 210), in which a shepherd boy raises the alarm about a wolf so many times when there is none that nobody believes him when the wolf finally comes (Wikipedia). An automated detector is that boy: it sometimes cries “species!” when the species is absent. Ignoring the false alarms biases occupancy estimates, and discarding every alarm wastes the true ones. crywolf takes the middle path: it uses a verified subset of detections to estimate how often the detector cries wolf, and corrects for it.

The logo is a nod to the 1980s and to “Cry Wolf”, the 1986 single by the Norwegian band a-ha from the album Scoundrel Days. It borrows the synthwave look of the decade: a neon magenta frame on deep purple, a striped setting sun, and a rounded display typeface. The wolf howls in sound waves over a cyan audio equalizer, standing for the acoustic recordings behind the package. The package has no connection with the band, and the logo uses none of its artwork or lyrics.

License

GPL (>= 3). The wolf silhouette in the logo is Canis lupus monstrabilis by Tracy A. Heath, from PhyloPic, in the public domain (CC0 1.0).
